claim: Brain development is regulated by conserved transcriptional programs across species.
source: Brain development is regulated by conserved transcriptional programs across species, but little is known about the divergent mechanisms that create species-specific characteristics.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain development presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Little is known about the divergent mechanisms that create species-specific characteristics in brain development.
source: Brain development is regulated by conserved transcriptional programs across species, but little is known about the divergent mechanisms that create species-specific characteristics.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Human cerebellar histogenesis differs in complexity compared with nonhuman primates and rodents.
source: Among brain regions, human cerebellar histogenesis differs in complexity compared with nonhuman primates and rodents, making it important to develop methods to generate human cerebellar neurons that closely resemble those in the developing human cerebellum.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work (Haldipur et al., 2019) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: The study reports a rapid protocol for the derivation of the human ATOH1 lineage from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs).
source: We report a rapid protocol for the derivation of the human ATOH1 lineage, the precursor of excitatory cerebellar neurons, from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: hPSC-derived cerebellar granule cells migrated along glial fibers upon transplantation into juvenile mice.
source: Upon transplantation into juvenile mice, hPSC-derived cerebellar granule cells migrated along glial fibers and integrated into the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transplantation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: hPSC-derived cerebellar granule cells integrated into the cerebellar cortex upon transplantation into juvenile mice.
source: Upon transplantation into juvenile mice, hPSC-derived cerebellar granule cells migrated along glial fibers and integrated into the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transplantation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is an unexpected temporal shift in the expression of RBFOX3 (NeuN) in the human outer external granule layer.
source: By Translational Ribosome Affinity Purification-seq, we identified an unexpected temporal shift in the expression of RBFOX3 (NeuN) and NEUROD1, which are classically associated with differentiated neurons, in the human outer external granule layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TRAP-seq data and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is an unexpected temporal shift in the expression of NEUROD1 in the human outer external granule layer.
source: By Translational Ribosome Affinity Purification-seq, we identified an unexpected temporal shift in the expression of RBFOX3 (NeuN) and NEUROD1, which are classically associated with differentiated neurons, in the human outer external granule layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TRAP-seq data and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: RBFOX3 (NeuN) and NEUROD1 are classically associated with differentiated neurons.
source: By Translational Ribosome Affinity Purification-seq, we identified an unexpected temporal shift in the expression of RBFOX3 (NeuN) and NEUROD1, which are classically associated with differentiated neurons, in the human outer external granule layer.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The molecular divergence in RBFOX3 and NEUROD1 expression may enable the protracted development of the human cerebellum compared to mice.
source: This molecular divergence may enable the protracted development of the human cerebellum compared to mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract.

claim: The human cerebellum contributes to cognitive functions.
source: The human cerebellum is now recognized to contribute to cognitive functions (Allen et al., 1997; Carta et al., 2019; Fiez, 1996; Schmahmann et al., 2019; Stoodley et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017), in addition to a critical role in motor control and motor learning.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The human cerebellum has a critical role in motor control and motor learning.
source: The human cerebellum is now recognized to contribute to cognitive functions (Allen et al., 1997; Carta et al., 2019; Fiez, 1996; Schmahmann et al., 2019; Stoodley et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017), in addition to a critical role in motor control and motor learning.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cerebellum is one of the most ancient cortical regions.
source: As one of the most ancient cortical regions, the cerebellum also appears central to human cognitive evolution, having rapidly expanded in absolute size, and relative to the neocortex in apes and humans (Barton and Venditti, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cerebellum appears central to human cognitive evolution.
source: As one of the most ancient cortical regions, the cerebellum also appears central to human cognitive evolution, having rapidly expanded in absolute size, and relative to the neocortex in apes and humans (Barton and Venditti, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Barton and Venditti, 2014.

claim: The cerebellum has rapidly expanded in absolute size in apes and humans.

claim: The cerebellum has rapidly expanded relative to the neocortex in apes and humans.

claim: Recent studies provide evidence of the complexity of human cerebellar histogenesis compared with nonhuman primates and rodents.
source: Recent studies provide evidence of the complexity of human cerebellar histogenesis compared with nonhuman primates and rodents (Haldipur et al., 2019), making it important to develop methods to generate human cerebellar neurons to model human development and disease.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Haldipur et al., 2019.

claim: The cerebellar cortex develops from rhombomere 1.
source: The cerebellar cortex develops from rhombomere 1 (Wingate and Hatten, 1999) with a primary germinal zone that produces the Purkinje neurons and interneurons, and a secondary germinal zone, marked by the ATOH1 transcription factor, that emerges from the rhombic lip and generates cerebellar granule cells (GCs) (Hatten and Heintz, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wingate and Hatten, 1999.

claim: The primary germinal zone of the cerebellar cortex produces Purkinje neurons and interneurons.
source: The cerebellar cortex develops from rhombomere 1 (Wingate and Hatten, 1999) with a primary germinal zone that produces the Purkinje neurons and interneurons, and a secondary germinal zone, marked by the ATOH1 transcription factor, that emerges from the rhombic lip and generates cerebellar granule cells (GCs) (Hatten and Heintz, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A secondary germinal zone marked by the ATOH1 transcription factor emerges from the rhombic lip.

evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hatten and Heintz, 1995.

claim: The secondary germinal zone marked by ATOH1 generates cerebellar granule cells (GCs).

evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hatten and Heintz, 1995.

claim: Prior to the specification of granule cell progenitors, the ATOH1 lineage gives rise to a subset of hindbrain nuclei and cerebellar nuclei in mice.
source: Importantly, prior to the specification of granule cell progenitors (GCPs), the ATOH1 lineage gives rise to a subset of hindbrain nuclei and cerebellar nuclei in mice (Machold and Fishell, 2005; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Machold and Fishell, 2005 and Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Previous studies have mostly focused on generating human Purkinje cells from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs).
source: While previous studies have mostly focused on generating human Purkinje cells (Buchholz et al., 2020; Erceg et al., 2010; Muguruma et al., 2015; Nayler et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2018) from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), little attention has been given to defining the molecular pathways that generate human GCs and other rhombic lip derivatives.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Little attention has been given to defining the molecular pathways that generate human GCs and other rhombic lip derivatives.
source: While previous studies have mostly focused on generating human Purkinje cells (Buchholz et al., 2020; Erceg et al., 2010; Muguruma et al., 2015; Nayler et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2018) from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), little attention has been given to defining the molecular pathways that generate human GCs and other rhombic lip derivatives.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field based on literature review.

claim: GCPs are a known cell of origin for medulloblastoma.
source: The importance of understanding the human ATOH1 lineage is underscored by the fact that GCPs are a known cell of origin for medulloblastoma, the most common metastatic childhood brain tumor (Behesti and Marino, 2009; Marino et al., 2000), and GCs are implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders including autism (Bauman, 1991; Kloth et al., 2015; Menashe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Behesti and Marino, 2009 and Marino et al., 2000.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Chambers et al., 2009 and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Midbrain progenitors that express EN2 do not express ATOH1/PAX6.
source: Midbrain progenitors that express EN2 do not express ATOH1/PAX6 (Akazawa et al., 1995; Allan Brain Atlas), and dorsal posterior hindbrain/spinal cord Atoh1+ never express EN2 (Davidson et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Akazawa et al., 1995, Allan Brain Atlas, and Davidson et al., 1988.

claim: Dorsal posterior hindbrain/spinal cord Atoh1+ cells never express EN2.
source: Midbrain progenitors that express EN2 do not express ATOH1/PAX6 (Akazawa et al., 1995; Allan Brain Atlas), and dorsal posterior hindbrain/spinal cord Atoh1+ never express EN2 (Davidson et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Davidson et al., 1988.

claim: ATOH1-EGFP-;PAX6+,NeuN+ cells are indicative of differentiated GCs.
source: These analyses revealed the presence of ATOH1-EGFP-;PAX6+,NeuN+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, asterisk), indicative of differentiated GCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge of GC markers.

claim: A small number of Calretinin+ cells are indicative of cerebellar nuclei or unipolar brush cells.
source: A small number of Calretinin+ cells, indicative of cerebellar nuclei or unipolar brush cells (Abbott and Jacobowitz, 1995; Fujita et al., 2020; Wizeman et al., 2019), and ATOH1-EGFP-;SOX2+ cells (28 ± 16% [mean ± 1 SD of the SOX2+ cells, n = 2]), indicative of cells deriving from the ventricular zone neuroepithelium in the developing cerebellum (GABAergic lineage, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Abbott and Jacobowitz, 1995; Fujita et al., 2020; Wizeman et al., 2019.

claim: ATOH1-EGFP-;SOX2+ cells (28 ± 16% of the SOX2+ cells) are indicative of cells deriving from the ventricular zone neuroepithelium in the developing cerebellum (GABAergic lineage).
source: A small number of Calretinin+ cells, indicative of cerebellar nuclei or unipolar brush cells (Abbott and Jacobowitz, 1995; Fujita et al., 2020; Wizeman et al., 2019), and ATOH1-EGFP-;SOX2+ cells (28 ± 16% [mean ± 1 SD of the SOX2+ cells, n = 2]), indicative of cells deriving from the ventricular zone neuroepithelium in the developing cerebellum (GABAergic lineage, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and interpretation based on established knowledge.

claim: A great majority of the SOX2+ cells were ATOH1-EGFP+ (72 ± 16.7%).
source: Interestingly, a great majority of the SOX2+ cells were ATOH1-EGFP+ (72 ± 16.7% [mean ±1 SD, n = 2]; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: In the developing mouse cerebellum, SOX2 is abundantly expressed throughout the ventricular zone neuroepithelium, but is a rare find in the EGL.
source: In the developing mouse cerebellum, SOX2 is abundantly expressed throughout the ventricular zone neuroepithelium, but is a rare find in the EGL (Sutter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sutter et al., 2010.

claim: GCPs have extensive proliferative capacity in response to sonic hedgehog (SHH) in the postnatal mouse cerebellum.
source: A defining feature of GCPs is their extensive proliferative capacity in response to sonic hedgehog (SHH) in the postnatal mouse cerebellum (Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Lewis et al., 2004; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Lewis et al., 2004; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999.

claim: EdU uptake was significantly increased in the ATOH1-EGFP+ cells after treatment with SAG compared to control.
source: EdU uptake, a measure of cell proliferation, was significantly increased in the ATOH1-EGFP+ cells (Figure 1G) after treatment with SAG (an agonist of SHH signaling) compared to control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The hPSC-ATOH1+ lineage displayed similar dynamics in gene expression over time as seen in the mouse embryo (albeit extended in period).
source: In conclusion, the hPSC-ATOH1+ lineage displayed similar dynamics in gene expression over time as seen in the mouse embryo (albeit extended in period) and produced GCPs, which respond to SAG, by DIV23–28.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hPSC-ATOH1+ lineage produced GCPs, which respond to SAG, by DIV23–28.
source: In conclusion, the hPSC-ATOH1+ lineage displayed similar dynamics in gene expression over time as seen in the mouse embryo (albeit extended in period) and produced GCPs, which respond to SAG, by DIV23–28.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Compared to previously reported methods, both the speed (35 days versus 16 days) and the yield (from 17% to 80%) of GCP production were increased.
source: Compared to previously reported methods, both the speed (35 days versus 16 days) and the yield (from 17% to 80%) of GCP production were increased.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work based on experimental data from this study.

claim: In the mouse, early postmitotic GCs switch off Atoh1 and transiently express TAG1 in the inner EGL.
source: In the mouse, early postmitotic GCs switch off Atoh1 and transiently express TAG1 in the inner EGL.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: TAG1 was expressed already at DIV18, after which its expression increased.
source: In our cultures, TAG1 was expressed already at DIV18, after which its expression increased (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) using an antibody against TAG1 yielded 13 ± 7% TAG1+ cells at DIV28.
source: Magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) using an antibody against TAG1, which is expressed on the cell surface, yielded 13 ± 7% (n = 7) TAG1+ cells at DIV28 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: By DIV3 in co-culture, the majority of the TAG1+ cells were PAX6+.
source: TAG1+ cells were then co-cultured with either mixed cerebellar mouse neurons or glia to provide a permissive differentiation environment. By DIV3 in co-culture, the majority of the TAG1+ cells were PAX6+ (Figure 2D, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The TAG1- fraction contained mostly cells with larger nuclei that were PAX6-.
source: By contrast, the TAG1- fraction contained mostly cells with larger nuclei that were PAX6- (Figure 2D, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: By DIV20 co-culture (DIV48 total days) of TAG1+ cells with mouse neurons or glia, a majority of the human cells displayed characteristic GC morphology (60%).
source: By DIV20, co-culture (DIV48 total days) of TAG1+ cells with mouse neurons or glia resulted in a majority of the human cells displaying characteristic GC morphology, namely a small (<10 um) round nucleus and a limited number of extended processes (3–4) including bifurcated axons (Figure 2E, 136/230 examined, 60%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The human cells expressed the GC marker NEUROD1 (75%).
source: The human cells expressed the GC markers NEUROD1 (42/56 examined, 75%, Figure 2E) and PAX6 (174/218 examined, 80%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The human cells expressed the GC marker PAX6 (80%).
source: The human cells expressed the GC markers NEUROD1 (42/56 examined, 75%, Figure 2E) and PAX6 (174/218 examined, 80%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: All examined cells that expressed PAX6 (81%) also expressed NEUROD1.
source: In double-labeling experiments, all examined cells that expressed PAX6 (18/22, 81%) also expressed NEUROD1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Presynaptic specializations were apparent in neurons grown in co-culture with mouse glia only.
source: Interestingly, presynaptic specializations were apparent in neurons grown in co-culture with mouse glia only, indicating that cross-species neuron-glia interactions are sufficient to trigger synapse initiation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Cross-species neuron-glia interactions are sufficient to trigger synapse initiation.
source: Interestingly, presynaptic specializations were apparent in neurons grown in co-culture with mouse glia only, indicating that cross-species neuron-glia interactions are sufficient to trigger synapse initiation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The expression of vesicular glutamate receptor 1 (VGLUT1) was detected.
source: In addition, the expression of vesicular glutamate receptor 1 (VGLUT1), a presynaptic marker that in the cerebellum is localized to GC parallel fiber-Purkinje cell excitatory synapses, was detected (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: VGLUT1 is a presynaptic marker that in the cerebellum is localized to GC parallel fiber-Purkinje cell excitatory synapses.
source: In addition, the expression of vesicular glutamate receptor 1 (VGLUT1), a presynaptic marker that in the cerebellum is localized to GC parallel fiber-Purkinje cell excitatory synapses, was detected (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: TAG1-sorted cells integrated into the neonatal mouse cerebellar cortex.
source: Importantly, TAG1-sorted cells integrated into the neonatal mouse cerebellar cortex and migrated along glial fibers with stereotypical morphology of migrating neurons passaging through the EGL to settle in the internal granule cell layer (IGL) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAG1-sorted cells migrated along glial fibers with stereotypical morphology of migrating neurons passaging through the EGL to settle in the internal granule cell layer (IGL).
source: Importantly, TAG1-sorted cells integrated into the neonatal mouse cerebellar cortex and migrated along glial fibers with stereotypical morphology of migrating neurons passaging through the EGL to settle in the internal granule cell layer (IGL) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAG1-sorted cells displayed the stereotypical elongated morphology of migrating neurons on glia when co-cultured with glia isolated from the mouse cerebellum for 36 hr.
source: Moreover, we observed the stereotypical elongated morphology of migrating neurons on glia when TAG1-sorted cells were co-cultured with glia isolated from the mouse cerebellum (Figure 3B) for 36 hr, similar to previous observations with mouse GCs (Hatten, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Hatten, 1985.

claim: Cells that were not attached to glia displayed more rounded morphologies.
source: By contrast, cells that were not attached to glia displayed more rounded morphologies (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The DIV28 hPSC-GCs can undergo glial-guided migration both in vitro and upon transplantation in vivo.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that the DIV28 hPSC-GCs can undergo glial-guided migration both in vitro and upon transplantation in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An EGFP-tagged L10a ribosomal subunit was driven by the human ATOH1 enhancer, enabling GFP-mediated immunoprecipitation (IP) of ribosomally attached mRNAs in the ATOH1 lineage specifically.
source: An EGFP-tagged L10a ribosomal subunit was driven by the human ATOH1 enhancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), enabling GFP-mediated immunoprecipitation (IP) of ribosomally attached mRNAs in the ATOH1 lineage specifically.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TRAP bypasses the need for cell dissociation.
source: Importantly, this method bypasses the need for cell dissociation and provides information about transcripts, including the 3′UTR, that are present in both the cell soma and processes.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the TRAP methodology.

claim: TRAP provides information about transcripts, including the 3′UTR, that are present in both the cell soma and processes.
source: Importantly, this method bypasses the need for cell dissociation and provides information about transcripts, including the 3′UTR, that are present in both the cell soma and processes.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the TRAP methodology.

claim: TRAP-seq was performed at DIV28 when the ATOH1 lineage coexpressed GCP markers and displayed increased proliferation in response to SAG.
source: TRAP followed by RNA sequencing (TRAP-seq) was performed at DIV28 when the ATOH1 lineage coexpressed GCP markers and displayed increased proliferation in response to SAG (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ATOH1 transcript was enriched in IPs compared to the input.
source: The ATOH1 transcript was indeed enriched in IPs compared to the input (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Several GCP markers were enriched in IPs, while markers of differentiated GCs were depleted.
source: Several other GCP markers were similarly enriched, while markers of differentiated GCs were depleted (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Heatmaps of the major signaling pathways in development (WNT, BMP, SHH, FGF, HIPPO) highlighted enrichment of the WNT pathway in particular.
source: Heatmaps of the major signaling pathways in development (WNT, BMP, SHH, FGF, HIPPO) highlighted enrichment of the WNT pathway in particular (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed axon guidance, the WNT pathway, neuronal migration, and cell division among the top significantly enriched developmental processes.
source: Interestingly, gene ontology analysis revealed axon guidance, the WNT pathway, neuronal migration, and cell division among the top significantly enriched developmental processes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of the TRAP-seq data.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed that the DIV28 ATOH1 lineage most closely matched the profile of the 13–17 PCW human cerebellum.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed that the DIV28 ATOH1 lineage most closely matched the profile of the 13–17 PCW human cerebellum (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Comparisons to published single-cell RNA-seq data from the developing mouse cerebellum revealed most resemblance to various cerebellar glutamatergic lineages.
source: Moreover, comparisons to published single-cell RNA-seq data from the developing mouse cerebellum revealed most resemblance to various cerebellar glutamatergic lineages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no resemblance to glia or endothelial cells.
source: There was no resemblance to glia or endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TRAP-seq data closely match the developing human cerebellum.
source: Together, these analyses provide the first translational dataset for the hPSC-derived ATOH1 lineage. While the data closely match the developing human cerebellum, development appears accelerated in culture.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Development appears accelerated in culture compared to the developing human cerebellum.
source: Together, these analyses provide the first translational dataset for the hPSC-derived ATOH1 lineage. While the data closely match the developing human cerebellum, development appears accelerated in culture.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: TRAP-seq analysis of the ATOH1 lineage revealed the expression of several genes that are classically associated with postmitotic GCs in mice including RBFOX3 (encodes for the NeuN antigen) and NEUROD1.
source: In a surprising finding, TRAP-seq analysis of the ATOH1 lineage revealed the expression of several genes that are classically associated with postmitotic GCs in mice including RBFOX3 (encodes for the NeuN antigen) and NEUROD1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The coexpression of NEUROD1 and ATOH1 was confirmed by RT-PCR in IPs.
source: The coexpression of NEUROD1 and ATOH1 was confirmed by RT-PCR in IPs (Figure 5A) and in FAC-sorted EGFP+ cells derived from the ATOH1-EGFP line (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ATOH1-EGFP+ cells expressed NeuN and NEUROD1 by immunohistochemistry.
source: By immunohistochemistry, ATOH1-EGFP+ cells expressed NeuN and NEUROD1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Many outer EGL cells in the human, where the ATOH1+ progenitors reside, expressed both NEUROD1 and NeuN.
source: In contrast to the mouse, many outer EGL cells in the human, where the ATOH1+ progenitors reside (Haldipur et al., 2019), expressed both NEUROD1 (Figure 5B and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and NeuN (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B, C, and D.

claim: Ki67 was not as prevalent at 17 PCW in the human EGL as it is in the P0 mouse cerebellum.
source: Moreover, Ki67, a marker of proliferating cells, was not as prevalent at this stage in the human EGL as it is in the P0 mouse cerebellum (Figure 5B, high magnification, and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: In the human EGL, Ki67 expression was sparser, Ki67 and NEUROD1 coexpression was clearly evident, and there was no clear separation of cells into two layers as seen in the mouse.
source: In the human EGL, Ki67 expression was sparser, Ki67 and NEUROD1 coexpression was clearly evident, and there was no clear separation of cells into two layers as seen in the mouse.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Extensive examination of multiple stages of development in the mouse (from E15.5 until P6) and multiple regions of the developing cerebellum revealed very few NEUROD1+ cells at the pial surface of the EGL.
source: Extensive examination of multiple stages of development in the mouse (from E15.5 until P6) and multiple regions of the developing cerebellum revealed very few NEUROD1+ cells at the pial surface of the EGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Only at P6, a relatively late stage of cerebellar development in the mouse, when GCP proliferation peaks (Ki67 throughout the EGL) and the EGL is at its thickest, was an increase in NEUROD1+ cells in the oEGL detected.
source: Only at P6, a relatively late stage of cerebellar development in the mouse, when GCP proliferation peaks (Ki67 throughout the EGL) and the EGL is at its thickest, did we detect an increase in NEUROD1+ cells in the oEGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Punctate NeuN expression was detected in the human oEGL but not at any stages or regions examined in the mouse.
source: Punctate NeuN expression was detected in the human oEGL but not at any stages or regions examined in the mouse (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SOX2 is extensively expressed in the human EGL.
source: Finally, since a large number of ATOH1-EGFP+ cells were SOX2+ in our cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D) we examined SOX2 expression in the 17 PCW human cerebellum and found that SOX2 is extensively expressed in the human EGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), in contrast to the mouse, where SOX2+ cells in the EGL are a rare find (Sutter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SOX2+ cells in the mouse EGL are a rare find.
source: Finally, since a large number of ATOH1-EGFP+ cells were SOX2+ in our cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D) we examined SOX2 expression in the 17 PCW human cerebellum and found that SOX2 is extensively expressed in the human EGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), in contrast to the mouse, where SOX2+ cells in the EGL are a rare find (Sutter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sutter et al., 2010.

claim: The data reveal marked species differences in the expression of transcriptional regulators in the EGL.
source: Together, these data reveal marked species differences and extensive coexpression of transcriptional regulators that have classically until now been ascribed to either progenitors or differentiating neurons based on mouse studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is extensive coexpression of transcriptional regulators that have classically until now been ascribed to either progenitors or differentiating neurons based on mouse studies.
source: Together, these data reveal marked species differences and extensive coexpression of transcriptional regulators that have classically until now been ascribed to either progenitors or differentiating neurons based on mouse studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The study reports a method for the scalable derivation of the human ATOH1 neuronal lineage from hPSCs that yields cerebellar progenitors by day 16 and GCs within 48 days in chemically defined medium.
source: We report a method for the scalable derivation of the human ATOH1 neuronal lineage from hPSCs that yields cerebellar progenitors by day 16 and GCs within 48 days in chemically defined medium.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The study provides a timeline of developmental progression of the human ATOH1 lineage by gene expression.
source: In contrast to previous methods for derivation of cerebellar neurons with a focus on Purkinje cells (Buchholz et al., 2020; Erceg et al., 2010; Muguruma et al., 2015; Nayler et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2018), we provide a timeline of developmental progression of the human ATOH1 lineage by gene expression and an unbiased comparison of the transcriptional profile to the developing human brain.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings of the study.

claim: The study provides an unbiased comparison of the transcriptional profile to the developing human brain.
source: In contrast to previous methods for derivation of cerebellar neurons with a focus on Purkinje cells (Buchholz et al., 2020; Erceg et al., 2010; Muguruma et al., 2015; Nayler et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2018), we provide a timeline of developmental progression of the human ATOH1 lineage by gene expression and an unbiased comparison of the transcriptional profile to the developing human brain.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings of the study.

claim: The expression of markers of the cerebellar nuclei (LHX9, LHX2) and the presence of Calretinin+ cells indicate the production of additional ATOH1 derivatives.
source: While our focus was derivation of GCs, the expression of markers of the cerebellar nuclei (LHX9, LHX2) and the presence of Calretinin+ cells indicate the production of additional ATOH1 derivatives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: MAC-sorted early postmitotic GCs (TAG1+) integrated into the mouse cerebellum and migrated through the EGL into the IGL in close apposition to glial fibers.
source: MAC-sorted early postmitotic GCs (TAG1+) integrated into the mouse cerebellum and migrated through the EGL into the IGL in close apposition to glial fibers, providing an in vivo system to study human GC migration and migration defects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: This is the first successful demonstration of migration followed by integration of hPSC-GCs into a stratified cortex.
source: This is the first successful demonstration of migration followed by integration of hPSC-GCs into a stratified cortex, suggesting that molecular pathways required for glial-guided migration have developed in the human cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Molecular pathways required for glial-guided migration have developed in the human cells.
source: This is the first successful demonstration of migration followed by integration of hPSC-GCs into a stratified cortex, suggesting that molecular pathways required for glial-guided migration have developed in the human cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the transplantation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Comparison of TRAP-seq data to RNA-seq data from the developing human brain matched the DIV28 hPSC-ATOH1 lineage to the human cerebellum at 13–17 PCW.
source: Comparison of our data to RNA-seq data from the developing human brain matched the DIV28 hPSC-ATOH1 lineage to the human cerebellum at 13–17 PCW.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Analysis of key developmental pathways revealed that the WNT pathway is particularly enriched.
source: Analysis of key developmental pathways revealed that the WNT pathway is particularly enriched.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TRAP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mouse genetic studies show that WNT signaling is critical for both early cerebellar development and later circuit establishment.
source: Indeed, mouse genetic studies show that WNT signaling is critical for both early cerebellar development and later circuit establishment (Lucas and Salinas, 1997; McMahon and Bradley, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lucas and Salinas, 1997 and McMahon and Bradley, 1990.

claim: The divergent expression of NEUROD1 and RBFOX3 in the human oEGL suggests an expansion of an 'intermediate' cellular state.
source: The divergent expression of NEUROD1 and RBFOX3 in the human oEGL suggests an expansion of an 'intermediate' cellular state that may serve to allow the progenitor pool to persist much longer, to enable the protracted period of cerebellar development in humans compared to mouse.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The expansion of an 'intermediate' cellular state may serve to allow the progenitor pool to persist much longer, to enable the protracted period of cerebellar development in humans compared to mouse.
source: The divergent expression of NEUROD1 and RBFOX3 in the human oEGL suggests an expansion of an 'intermediate' cellular state that may serve to allow the progenitor pool to persist much longer, to enable the protracted period of cerebellar development in humans compared to mouse.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Both NEUROD1 and RBFOX3 are expressed in early postmitotic as well as fully differentiated neurons, rarely in neuroblasts, across species and brain regions.
source: Both NEUROD1 and RBFOX3 are expressed in early postmitotic as well as fully differentiated neurons, rarely in neuroblasts, across species and brain regions (D'Amico et al., 2013; Lee et al., 1995; Miyata et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to D'Amico et al., 2013; Lee et al., 1995; Miyata et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of either NEUROD1 or RBFOX3 in progenitors induces neuronal differentiation.
source: Overexpression of either gene in progenitors induces neuronal differentiation (Boutin et al., 2010; Butts et al., 2014; Lee et al., 1995; Pataskar et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Boutin et al., 2010; Butts et al., 2014; Lee et al., 1995; Pataskar et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: In the Xenopus embryo, the coexpression of Atoh1 and NeuroD1 in the EGL has been reported.
source: Interestingly, in the Xenopus embryo, the coexpression of Atoh1 and NeuroD1 in the EGL has been reported, and it was hypothesized that both the timing of expression and the gene regulatory function of NEUROD1 have adapted to support development of a nonproliferative EGL (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Butts et al., 2014.

claim: It was hypothesized that both the timing of expression and the gene regulatory function of NEUROD1 have adapted to support development of a nonproliferative EGL in Xenopus.
source: Interestingly, in the Xenopus embryo, the coexpression of Atoh1 and NeuroD1 in the EGL has been reported, and it was hypothesized that both the timing of expression and the gene regulatory function of NEUROD1 have adapted to support development of a nonproliferative EGL (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Butts et al., 2014.

claim: The coexpression of NEUROD1 and RBFOX3 in GCPs, together with the more extensive expression of SOX2 in the human EGL, may enable an extended immature (stem cell) or quiescent state to preserve the progenitor pool.
source: In the human, we propose that the coexpression of these factors in GCPs, together with the more extensive expression of SOX2 in the human EGL, may enable an extended immature (stem cell) or quiescent state to preserve the progenitor pool.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Different levels of NEUROD1 and RBFOX3, in combination, may be important for proliferation versus quiescent states in the GCPs.
source: We speculate that different levels of each factor, in combination, may be important for proliferation versus quiescent states in the GCPs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Ki67 labeling showed fewer positive cells in the human EGL at 17 PCW than the comparable P0 mouse EGL, hinting at differences in proliferative regulation.
source: Indeed, Ki67 labeling showed fewer positive cells in the human EGL at 17 PCW than the comparable P0 mouse EGL, hinting at differences in proliferative regulation.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The findings, together with findings in the Xenopus and the differential proliferative capacity of the EGL in several vertebrate species, support the existence of evolutionary adaptations in EGL development across species.
source: Our findings, together with findings in the Xenopus and the differential proliferative capacity of the EGL in several vertebrate species (Iulianella et al., 2019), support the existence of evolutionary adaptations in EGL development across species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior work, supported by citation to Iulianella et al., 2019.
